messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

David is thirty-six, a retail worker at a large home-goods store in a suburban strip mall, and he has been married for seven years to a woman named Sarah. Three years ago, he was working security at a sold-out outdoor concert when a portable generator near the stage caught fire. The flames spread fast, and the crowd—already packed tight—surged toward the exits in a single, panicked mass. What David remembers most vividly are not the flames themselves but the way people behaved: grown men shoving women aside, a teenager climbing over a fallen couple, someone screaming that it was a terrorist attack when it was only a faulty wire. He was pinned against a metal barrier, the heat pressing his face, and he felt the grit of ash and burnt debris settle into the collar of his uniform—a coarse, greasy texture that clung to his skin and that he could not wash off for days afterward, no matter how many times he scrubbed. He got out, but the images stayed: a woman’s hand reaching, a child’s shoe left behind, each moment a still frame in his mind, sharper and more real than anything that has happened since.

At first he told himself it was not that bad—he survived, after all—and he tried hard not to think about it, filling his days with double shifts and late nights until he was too tired to dream. But the memories kept breaking through, and when they did, they brought a shame so thick it felt physical: he should have done more, should have stopped the stampede, should have been braver. Shame made the snapshots even harder to shake. He found that if he pressed his thumbnail into the web of his other hand, or dug the edge of a key into his forearm, the sharp pain would cut the memory short. Scratching became a habit, a private way to silence the thought, though the shame always came back later, heavier.

The crowds at the store have become unbearable. When a customer cuts in line or yells at a cashier, David feels a hot tightness in his chest and immediately tells himself the event was nowhere near that bad—magical thinking that lasts only a moment before he catches himself. The proximity of a busy aisle, with people pressing close to reach a discount sign, sends a vivid snapshot into his mind: the surge, the heat, the hand. Because those memories feel more real than the fluorescent lights and tile floor around him, the slightest cue—the coarse weave of a fire blanket on a shelf, the rough texture of a scratchy towel—triggers another picture, and another. Each time that happens, he tries to suppress the thought, but suppression only makes the next snapshot arrive sooner, sharper, and with more shame. He has realized that his effort to ignore the trauma actually makes him scan the aisles for potential reminders, so that now a mere glimpse of the blanket aisle sets off a cascade: the texture, the memory, the surge of shame, then the need to hurt himself to stop it.

Sarah has noticed the scratches on his arms and the way he flinches in crowds, but David cannot explain it. What finally brought him to a therapist was a scene at work last Tuesday: a customer knocked over a stack of bed linens, and as David bent to pick them up his fingertips brushed the rough cotton. He froze, saw the ash, felt the heat, and in front of a dozen people he scratched his forearm raw. His manager sent him home. That night, sitting in the dark living room, David told Sarah it was getting worse. He is terrified that if he stops trying to tell himself it was not that bad, the snapshots will flood him completely and he will never leave his house again. Yet he is equally afraid that the strategies he has built are the only thing keeping him from falling apart, and that without them he will have no way to hold the shame at bay.
